name: RISC-V International (formerly RISC-V Foundation)
origin_detail: The RISC-V ISA began at UC Berkeley in 2010 (Krste Asanovic, David Patterson and students). The RISC-V Foundation was set up in 2015 as a Delaware non-stock corporation; members voted in 2019 to move it, and it reincorporated in Switzerland as the RISC-V International Association in March 2020, citing the risk of government restrictions on an open standard.
flagship_projects: RISC-V unprivileged and privileged ISA specifications
openness_notes: Hardware column applied to what the organisation stewards: the ISA specifications. They are published under CC BY 4.0, described by RISC-V International as royalty-free, and developed by member working groups under a nonprofit board, so the standard itself is fully open with community (member) governance (4) from the Foundation's start to today. Caveats: governance weight scales with paid membership tier (dues up to $250k a year for Board plus TSC seats), and the open ISA does not make implementations open; most commercial cores are proprietary. Wikipedia says the original 2011 encoding was published 'all rights reserved' before the text moved to Creative Commons, so the pre-Foundation academic phase was briefly less open.

risk_events: 2019-2020: moved incorporation from Delaware to Switzerland over fears of US trade restrictions on an open standard
2023-11: eighteen US lawmakers urged export controls on RISC-V technology to limit Chinese use
2024-04: US Commerce Department said it was reviewing risks of China's RISC-V use; no formal restriction on the standard found in these searches
2026: approved as an ISO/IEC JTC1 PAS submitter, opening a route to an ISO standard (not yet ratified per searches)
robustness: High. A member-governed nonprofit owns the standard, specifications are CC BY 4.0, there are thousands of member organisations, and many competing implementers (SiFive, Andes, Alibaba T-Head, Nvidia, Western Digital, Google, and open cores such as Rocket and CVA6), so no single company's failure endangers the ISA. Main exposure is geopolitical: export-control pressure and fragmentation through proprietary extensions.
physical_science_relevance: A royalty-free ISA lets universities and labs tape out custom processors and instrument controllers without licence fees; open cores are widely used in research FPGAs and accelerators.
openness_effect_assessment: Opening the ISA under a neutral foundation turned a Berkeley teaching and research project into a standard with roughly 4,100-4,500 member organisations by 2024 and commercial backers from SiFive to Nvidia. Neutral governance mattered enough that members moved the body to Switzerland in 2020 to protect openness from US trade policy. Openness also made RISC-V the target of US export-control debates (2023-2024) precisely because Chinese firms can adopt it freely.
key_takeaway: RISC-V International shows the 'open standard, closed products' division of labour in hardware: a lean nonprofit (about $8.6M revenue in 2024) maintains a fully open, royalty-free specification while companies compete with proprietary implementations on top. It is the most robust governance form in this group, and its main risks are geopolitical rather than commercial.
